Economy · The Big Story

Japan’s price number fell. The pressure did not.

Wholesale inflation slowed to 6.8% in September and missed forecasts. Then one line in the Bank of Japan’s table changed the picture: nonferrous metals were 40.2% more expensive than a year earlier.

By Yuji Shimizu · YUJI @ Japan
Published October 13, 2026 · 14:20 JST · 9 min read

At 8:50 on Tuesday morning, the Bank of Japan published a number that looked like relief. Prices charged between Japanese companies were 6.8% higher in September than a year earlier. That was down from 7.6% in August and below the 7.6% median forecast collected by Reuters.

The month-to-month reading seemed calmer still. The domestic Corporate Goods Price Index, or CGPI, fell 0.3% from August, its second consecutive monthly decline. Rice and other agricultural products helped slow the annual rise. For a country that has spent years trying to distinguish healthy inflation from an imported cost shock, a lower number matters.

But this is not the price consumers see on a supermarket shelf, and it is not an all-clear. It is a snapshot of goods traded between companies: materials, machinery, fuel, food and thousands of other inputs before they travel through the supply chain. Some costs were cooling in September. Others were accelerating hard enough to remain a warning about what businesses may face next.

The headline was 6.8%. Nonferrous metals—including copper and aluminum—were up 40.2% from a year earlier. Japan’s inflation story did not disappear; it split into two very different stories.

Why 6.8% is both lower and high

The index is measured against the same month a year earlier, so today’s 6.8% compares September 2026 with September 2025. August’s revised 7.6% compared a different pair of months. A slower annual rate means the gap narrowed; it does not mean business prices became 6.8% cheaper. The index still says the average domestic basket cost substantially more than one year before.

The 0.3% monthly fall answers a separate question: did September move up or down from August? Two negative monthly readings suggest momentum eased recently. Yet monthly data can bounce with commodities, utilities, government support and seasonal supply. Analysts therefore read both comparisons rather than choosing the friendlier one.

+6.8%domestic corporate goods prices, year on year
−0.3%change from August, second monthly fall
+40.2%nonferrous metals, year on year

The forecast miss adds a third layer. Economists polled by Reuters had expected 7.6%, equal to August’s rate. The lower result means the September cooling was stronger than their median estimate. It can influence expectations about inflation and the Bank of Japan, but one wholesale release cannot decide monetary policy by itself. Wages, consumer prices, services, demand and expectations all matter.

The copper line reaches farther than a mine

Nonferrous metals cover metals other than iron and steel. Copper and aluminum run through power grids, vehicles, buildings, electronics and data centers. Copper demand is especially sensitive to electrification and infrastructure; the global expansion of computing capacity for artificial intelligence adds another potential source of demand. Reuters noted that strong AI-related demand may be contributing to copper prices.

Japan imports much of the raw material and energy its manufacturers need. That exposes domestic businesses to two prices at once: the world commodity price and the exchange rate at which they buy it. A weaker yen can make a dollar-priced input costlier even when its overseas quotation is unchanged. That transmission is why import prices deserve attention alongside the domestic index.

In September, the yen-based import price index was 24.5% higher than a year earlier, according to the Bank of Japan data reported by Reuters. That was slightly below August’s 25.1% rise, but still a large increase. Import prices are not a promise that consumer prices will rise by the same amount. They are an upstream pressure that companies can absorb, offset, delay or pass on.

The route from copper to a household is indirect. A cable maker pays more for material. A contractor pays more for cable. A building, factory or data-center project becomes more expensive. Some firms accept smaller margins; others renegotiate contracts or redesign products. The effect may arrive months later, and it will differ by industry.

Rice cooled one number, not every grocery bill

Agricultural, forestry and fishery products pulled down the annual rate, with rice central to the change. That matters because rice is culturally and economically unlike an anonymous industrial input: it is a staple, a farm income, a political concern and a price noticed immediately by households. A decline at the corporate-goods stage can reduce one source of food pressure.

Still, the CGPI does not say every bag of rice at every store became cheaper today. Retail prices include processing, packaging, logistics, labor, rent and the timing of inventory contracts. Old, more expensive stock can remain on shelves while wholesale conditions change. Different varieties and regions also move differently.

This is the mistake to avoid: reading the index as a receipt. The CGPI is designed to measure prices at the producer and wholesale stages. Japan’s consumer price index is the better measure of what households pay. The two are connected, but neither moves instantly or evenly with the other.

Why companies may still raise prices

Companies decide whether to pass on costs based on margins, contracts and competition. A large exporter with currency earnings can experience a weak yen differently from a small domestic firm importing material. A restaurant can shrink portions, change suppliers or raise a menu price. A manufacturer can hedge currencies or sign long-term metal contracts. An average index hides all of those decisions.

The September report therefore contains a tension. Aggregate momentum slowed, partly because one highly visible food category cooled. At the same time, globally traded materials remained expensive and import prices rose by almost one quarter from a year earlier in yen terms. The businesses most exposed to those inputs do not experience “6.8%” as an average; they experience their own invoice.

For workers, the question is whether wages keep pace with the consumer prices that emerge at the end of this chain. On October 9, the Statistics Bureau reported that August spending by two-or-more-person households fell 3.1% in real terms from a year earlier even though nominal spending rose. That earlier release showed the downstream side of the same problem: more yen can buy less when prices outpace income.

What happens next

The next test is persistence. If monthly producer prices keep falling and import-price growth continues to ease, companies may face less pressure to raise prices later. If copper, aluminum, fuel or the yen move the other way, the calm headline could prove temporary. Revisions also matter: today’s September figure is preliminary, not final.

The Bank of Japan will compare these costs with consumer inflation, wage settlements and economic activity. A below-forecast CGPI may modestly soften expectations of immediate price pressure, but the 40.2% metals increase argues against treating a single slowdown as victory. Monetary policy responds to a pattern, not a dramatic cell in one table.

For readers outside Japan, today’s most useful insight is that “inflation” is not one number. Japan can have falling rice prices at the wholesale stage, soaring metal costs, a weaker monthly average and a still-large annual rise at the same time. Each describes a different link in the chain.

The Japanese term for that chain’s first number is 企業物価 (kigyō bukka): “corporate goods prices.” 企業 means company or enterprise; 物価 means the general level of prices. It belongs mainly to economic news, not everyday shopping conversation. A natural headline phrase is kigyō bukka ga jōshō shita—corporate goods prices rose. DraMap is built around learning Japanese in context; today, that context begins with an invoice before it reaches a receipt.

So the lower number deserves attention, but not celebration. September’s report says pressure became less uniform. The average slowed. The supply chain did not.
